definition: Embodied cognition represents a diverse group of theories which investigate how cognition is shaped by the bodily state and capacities of the organism.
details: These embodied factors include the motor system, the perceptual system, bodily interactions with the environment (situatedness), and the assumptions about the world that shape the functional structure of the brain and body of the organism. Embodied cognition suggests that these elements are essential to a wide spectrum of cognitive functions, such as perception biases, memory recall, comprehension and high-level mental constructs (such as meaning attribution and categories) and performance on various cognitive tasks (reasoning or judgment). The embodied mind thesis challenges other theories, such as cognitivism, computationalism, and Cartesian dualism. It is closely related to the extended mind thesis, situated cognition, and enactivism. The modern version depends on understandings drawn from up-to-date research in psychology, linguistics, cognitive science, dynamical systems, artificial intelligence, robotics, animal cognition, plant cognition, and neurobiology.

explainer.lead: Embodied cognition is the idea that thinking is shaped not just by the brain, but by the whole body and its interactions with its surroundings. It matters because perception, memory, reasoning, and action may depend on what an agent's body can sense and do, rather than on abstract representations alone.

tiers.eli5: Learning to ride a bicycle is not just knowing facts in your head: your hands, legs, balance, and movements on the road all take part. Embodied cognition says thinking works somewhat like that more generally. What your body can sense and do helps shape how you understand and respond to things.
tiers.practitioner: In AI and robotics, an embodied approach treats sensors, motor capacities, and ongoing interaction with the environment as central to cognition, not merely as inputs and outputs attached to an isolated planner. Related work draws on dynamical systems, psychology, cognitive science, and neurobiology, with knowledge aimed at guiding behavior as surroundings change. A key pitfall is treating embodied cognition as one precise method, or confusing it with extended and situated cognition, when it is a broad research program with weaker and stronger variants.
tiers.paperLevel: In its narrower form, the embodiment thesis states that many features of cognition depend deeply on characteristics of an agent's physical body, such that the beyond-the-brain body plays a significant causal or physically constitutive role in cognitive processing. Cognition is constrained by the system's goals and capacities, involves information processing, and serves action through exploration and modification of the environment rather than simply maximizing representational accuracy. It is better understood as a research program than a unified theory, and it remains conceptually distinct from extended cognition, which places processing partly in the world, and situated cognition, which emphasizes probing, changing, and sociocultural interactions.

explainer.example: Consider a robot exploring an unfamiliar room. Its sensors and possible movements determine what it can perceive, so it changes position and gathers new information as conditions change; that information guides its next action. On an embodied account, cognition lies in this body–environment activity, not only in an internal map or plan.

usedIn.name: Robotics
usedIn.detail: Connects cognition to a robot's bodily capacities, sensorimotor activity, and changing surroundings.

usedIn.name: Artificial intelligence
usedIn.detail: Offers an alternative to accounts based solely on abstract representations, internal world models, and planning.

usedIn.name: Cognitive science and psychology
usedIn.detail: Informs research into perception, memory, reasoning, problem solving, and mental imagery.

usedIn.name: Neuroscience
usedIn.detail: Supports accounts in which successful behavior integrates sensorimotor, cognitive, and affective capacities.

explainer.intuition: A mind is not necessarily an isolated brain manipulating abstract representations. The body's senses and movements, together with its ongoing exchanges with the environment, can help constitute and guide cognition.
howItWorks: Start with the agent's particular body, perceptual system, and motor capacities.
Sense the surroundings through the possibilities and limits those capacities provide.
Explore and modify the environment through situated bodily interaction.
Transform incoming information to guide behavior toward the system's goals, rather than merely building maximally accurate representations.
Let these bodily and environmental relations shape perception, attention, memory, reasoning, and other cognitive features.
explainer.whyItMatters: Embodied cognition challenges cognitivism, computationalism, and Cartesian dualism by restoring bodily experience to accounts of the mind. It also reframes successful real-world behavior as emerging from the relationship between an agent and the opportunities its environment provides.
misconceptions: It does not claim that the brain is unimportant; it argues that the body beyond the brain also plays a significant role.
It is not identical to the extended mind thesis, which extends cognitive processing outward into the agent's world.
It is not one settled, unified theory, but a broad research program containing different claims and degrees of embodiment.

diagram.caption: Cognition unfolds through a continuing loop among bodily capacities, information processing, action, and the environment.
